summary: Describes plans by Computer Corporation of America and the Dynamics Modeling System group at MIT's Project MAC to store data about ARPANET host behavior, collected by a program called SURVEY, in CCA's datacomputer. An interactive program would then retrieve it.

plainLanguage.summary: Researchers wanted to keep a big pile of measurements about the network in a computer built to store data, and look it up later with a program.

questions: what was survey on the arpanet
subtitle: Archiving network measurements in a specialized database

tldr.problem: The SURVEY program was collecting detailed ARPANET host status information but discarding most of it daily, retaining only summaries and losing potentially useful details.
tldr.mechanism: MIT and CCA built a system to transmit SURVEY's data to CCA's datacomputer, which stores it with indices organized by host, status, month, and year. A retrieval program called SURRET allows interactive queries using boolean expressions to select subsets of the data.
tldr.outcome: From July 1973 onwards, all detailed survey data has been preserved and available for analysis through an interactive query tool, enabling historical tracking of network host behavior.

today: RFC 565 documents an early network monitoring and data preservation system from 1973. It represents an early approach to collecting and analyzing network health metrics over time.

sections.title: The SURVEY Program and Data Collection
sections.content:
In late 1971, the Dynamics Modeling System (DMS) group at MIT began running SURVEY, a program that continuously monitors the health and responsiveness of ARPANET hosts. Every twenty minutes, SURVEY attempts an initial connection to the logger socket (socket 1) of each of 28 network hosts from a PDP-10 computer at DMS. For each host, it records a date, time, host identifier, status, and response time in tenths of seconds.

Host status is recorded in one of six states: undetermined/not surveyed, disconnected from network, network control program not responding, initial connection protocol aborted by host, initial connection timed out, or logger available and responding. The full dataset from 28 hosts creates 476 characters of data per survey cycle, and with 72 surveys per day, the datacomputer receives approximately 34,272 characters daily from DMS.
sections.plainLanguage: SURVEY checks 28 computers every twenty minutes to see if they are working and how fast they answer. It writes down the date, time, host name, whether it worked, and how many tenths of seconds it took.

sections.title: Storage and Retrieval in the Datacomputer
sections.content:
CCA's datacomputer stores the SURVEY data with indices inverted by host, status, month, and year. This inversion allows the system to perform rapid boolean queries without consulting the raw data itself, substantially speeding up retrieval. The SURRET program, written in the MUDDLE language at DMS, provides an interactive interface for selecting data. Users specify criteria for five fields: host name, date, time, response time, and host status. They can specify individual values, groups of values, or upper and lower bounds, and request any subset of the five fields to be returned.

A sample SURRET session shows a user querying data for host CASE-10 on August 5, 1973, for times between 2000 and 2400 hours. The system returns formatted results showing time, status, and response time for each measurement point. The system compiles SURRET queries into a formal datalanguage and sends them to the datacomputer, which executes the query and formats results for display.
sections.plainLanguage: The datacomputer remembers data sorted by which computer, what status, and when. A tool called SURRET lets you type what you want: like "show me data for CASE-10 on August 5 between 8 PM and midnight." It gives you back a nice table.

sections.title: Interactive Query and Analysis
sections.content:
SURRET maintains a current state of five prospective retrieval criteria. Users change criteria by typing commands like HOST (CASE-10) and then request data with the REQ command. Commands like STATE display current values. Users can combine multiple criteria using boolean logic, such as HOST (CASE-10 OR USC-44), or issue multiple queries sequentially by updating criteria. The system's boolean indexing enables rapid filtering; queries against boolean expressions on the indices complete without needing to scan the entire dataset.

Detailed survey data from July 10, 1973 forward is available directly from the datacomputer or through SURRET, with documentation available through the NIC or by contacting CCA directly.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for "this host or that host" and the database finds them fast. You can also ask for times in a range or specific dates. The whole query system is fast because of clever indexing.
